description: Width tiers for Mathematics Year 9 — ACARA v9. One entry per descriptor code.
subject: Mathematics

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest engagement that satisfies the descriptor's command term. For understanding/concept descriptors: minimum phenomena or contexts. For modelling and investigation descriptors: the narrowest single context that completes the full cycle.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope grounded in the most common elaboration cases. What a well-taught Year 9 class would reach.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, contexts or application domains — not harder versions of the same context. First Nations directions included wherever elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA v9 elaborations are used as source data for grounding typical_width and identifying wider directions. They are preserved verbatim in each entry as a source record.

AC9M9N01.minimum_width: Represent the real number system as a hierarchy (natural numbers, integers, rationals, irrationals); give one example of an irrational number and explain why it cannot be expressed as a fraction; solve one problem by substituting a real number into a formula.
AC9M9N01.typical_width: Represent the relationships between irrationals, rationals, integers and natural numbers; distinguish between exact representations (e.g. π, √2) and decimal approximations; use the real number line to represent solution intervals for linear inequalities; solve problems by substituting real numbers into formulas, expressing answers in exact and approximate form.
wider: Investigate the position of irrational numbers on the real number line using geometric constructions (e.g. locating √2 as the diagonal of a unit square)
Explore how ancient and First Nations mathematical traditions represented and worked with quantities that we now classify as irrational
Investigate the difference between algebraic and transcendental irrationals (e.g. √2 vs π) and what is known about their nature
elaborations: investigating the real number system by representing the relationships between irrationals, rationals, integers and natural numbers and discussing the difference between exact representations and approximate decimal representations of irrational numbers
using a real number line to indicate the solution interval for inequalities of the form ax+b<c or ax+b>c
using positive and negative rational numbers to solve problems; for example, for financial planning such as budgeting

solving problems involving the substitution of real numbers into formulas, understanding that solutions can be represented in exact form or as a decimal approximation, such as calculating the area of a circle using A=πr²
investigating the position of rational and irrational numbers on the real number line, using geometric constructions to locate rational numbers and square roots on a number line

AC9M9A01.minimum_width: Apply at least three exponent laws to simplify numerical expressions with positive and negative integer exponents; apply the same laws to simplify a simple algebraic expression with one variable.
AC9M9A01.typical_width: Apply all exponent laws (product, quotient, power of a power, zero exponent, negative exponent) to both numerical expressions and algebraic expressions involving products, quotients and powers of constants and variables; explain why negative exponents produce reciprocals; connect to SI unit prefixes.
wider: Represent decimals in expanded exponential form and connect to place value structure
Apply exponent laws in scientific contexts involving very large or very small quantities (e.g. SI prefixes from pico- to tera-)
Investigate how exponent laws underpin logarithmic relationships and connect to Year 10 work on surds and logarithms
elaborations: representing decimals in exponential form; e.g. 0.475 = 4×10⁻¹ + 7×10⁻² + 5×10⁻³
simplifying and evaluating numerical expressions involving both positive and negative integer exponents, explaining why; e.g. 5⁻³ = 1/5³ = 1/125
relating the computation of numerical expressions involving exponents to the exponent laws; e.g. 2³÷2⁵ = 2⁻² = 1/4 and (3×5)² = 9×25 = 225
recognising exponents in algebraic expressions and applying the relevant exponent laws; e.g. a⁰=1, x¹=x, 1/w × 1/w = w⁻²
relating simplification from first principles to exponent laws; e.g. (a²)³ = a⁶; b²×b³ = b⁵
applying the exponent laws to simplifying expressions involving products, quotients and powers of constants and variables; e.g. (2xy)³/xy⁴ = 8x²y⁻¹
relating the prefixes for SI units from pico- to tera- to the corresponding powers of 10

AC9M9A02.minimum_width: Expand one binomial product of the form (x+a)(x+b) where a and b are integers; factorise one monic quadratic expression x²+bx+c with integer roots.
AC9M9A02.typical_width: Expand all four combinations of binomials (both signs) and identify the general pattern (x+a)(x+b) = x²+(a+b)x+ab; factorise monic quadratic expressions x²+mx+n for integer m and n; recognise the relationship between expansion and factorisation as inverse operations; use area models or algebra tiles to represent both processes.
wider: Use digital tools to systematically explore factorisation patterns for x²+mx+n across a range of integer values of m and n, including non-factorisable cases
Investigate special cases: difference of squares (x+a)(x−a) = x²−a² and perfect square trinomials (x+a)² = x²+2ax+a²
Connect factorisation to solving quadratic equations and to graphical features of the parabola (x-intercepts)
elaborations: expanding combinations of binomials such as (x+7)(x+8), (x+7)(x−8), (x−7)(x+8), (x−7)(x−8) to identify expansion and factorisation patterns related to (x+a)(x+b) = x²+(a+b)x+ab, where a and b are integers
using manipulatives such as algebra tiles or area models to expand or factorise; e.g. (x+1)(x+3) = x²+4x+3, (x−5)² = x²−10x+25
recognising the relationship between expansion and factorisation, using digital tools to explore factorisation of x²+mx+n where m and n are integers

AC9M9A03.minimum_width: Calculate the gradient of a line segment between two given points; find the midpoint of a line interval; calculate the distance between two points using Pythagoras' theorem.
AC9M9A03.typical_width: Calculate gradient, midpoint and distance for any two points on the Cartesian plane using appropriate formulas; verify that gradient is independent of which two points on a line are chosen; use gradient relationships to identify parallel and perpendicular lines; interpret gradient as a constant rate of change in linear modelling contexts.
wider: Investigate gradients in real-world contexts using superimposed images (ramps, escalators, playground equipment) and connect to linear function rules
Explore how coordinate geometry underpins machine learning algorithms (e.g. linear regression, object detection) — discuss how gradient and distance calculations feature in these systems
Investigate how the midpoint formula and distance formula are used in geographic information systems (GIS) and mapping applications
elaborations: recognising that the gradient of a line is independent of which 2 distinct points on the line are used for the calculation
using digital tools to illustrate that parallel lines have the same gradient and that perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1
using Pythagoras' theorem to establish the distance between 2 points in the Cartesian plane
investigating graphical and algebraic techniques for finding the midpoint and gradient of a line segment between 2 points
using dynamic graphing software and superimposed real-world images to investigate gradients in context
investigating how coordinate geometry plays a role in machine learning and predictive algorithms such as object detection and navigation by autonomous vehicles

AC9M9A04.minimum_width: Identify a quadratic function from a table of values or equation; graph one quadratic function and identify its key features (turning point, axis of symmetry, x-intercepts if they exist); solve one monic quadratic equation with integer roots algebraically using factorisation.
AC9M9A04.typical_width: Identify quadratic functions using second differences; graph quadratic functions using digital tools and interpret symmetry, turning point, maximum/minimum and intercepts; solve monic quadratic equations algebraically (factorisation, null factor law) and graphically; recognise that no x-intercepts means no real solutions; recognise that x²=a (a>0) has two solutions.
wider: Graph percentages of illumination of moon phases and connect to First Nations Australians' understandings of moon phases, discussing the quadratic-like shape of the illumination cycle
Investigate projectile motion contexts (e.g. paths of balls, water from a hose) and interpret turning point and intercepts in physical terms
Explore how the discriminant (b²−4ac, introduced informally) determines the number of real solutions, connecting to graphical cases with 0, 1 or 2 x-intercepts
elaborations: recognising that constant second differences in a table of values indicate a quadratic
graphing quadratic functions using digital tools; interpreting symmetry, turning point, maximum/minimum values
solving quadratic equations algebraically and comparing to graphical solutions
using graphs to determine solutions; recognising roots correspond to x-intercepts; if no x-intercepts, no real solutions
relating x-intercepts to factorised form using the null factor law; e.g. y = (x−2)(x−3) has x-intercepts at x=2 and x=3
recognising x²=a (a>0) has 2 solutions; e.g. x²=39 gives x=±√39 ≈ ±6.245
graphing percentages of illumination of moon phases in relation to First Nations Australians' understandings of moon phases

AC9M9A05.minimum_width: Formulate a problem involving change as either a linear or quadratic function (with justification of the choice); solve the problem; interpret the solution in terms of the original situation; state one limitation of the model.
AC9M9A05.typical_width: Apply the full mathematical modelling cycle (formulate → solve → interpret → evaluate) to at least two different applied contexts involving change — one using a linear model and one using a quadratic model; compare what each model captures and where each breaks down; report methods and findings clearly.
wider: Model the hunting techniques of First Nations Australians using quadratic functions, exploring the effect of varying the number of hunters and interpreting the turning point in context
Model financial contexts involving both fixed and variable components (e.g. trade quotes with call-out fees, profit/loss with fixed overhead) and compare the linear model to real-world outcomes
Model a situation where neither linear nor quadratic is a perfect fit; evaluate what the model gets right and wrong, and suggest how it could be improved
elaborations: modelling practical contexts using linear functions such as cooking times including resting or cooling times, or water leakage from water tanks
modelling measurement situations: perimeter and areas of rectangles where length is a linear function of width
modelling practical contexts using simple quadratic functions; interpreting turning point and intercepts; e.g. area, projectiles, parabolic mirrors
modelling financial contexts using linear functions; e.g. profit/loss, trade quotes with call-out fees
modelling situations involving change; e.g. temperature change, speed fluctuation, acceleration/deceleration
modelling the hunting techniques of First Nations Australians using quadratic functions and exploring the effect of increasing the number of hunters

AC9M9A06.minimum_width: Vary one parameter (a or b) in y=ax+b or y=ax² and describe the effect on the graph; make a generalisation about what each parameter controls.
AC9M9A06.typical_width: Systematically vary both parameters in linear and quadratic functions using digital tools; describe the effect of each parameter on the graph (stretch, reflection, translation); connect graphical transformations to the algebraic form including completed square form; generalise emerging patterns.
wider: Extend parameter variation to at least two additional function families (e.g. reciprocal y=1/x, square root y=√x, exponential y=aˣ) and identify which transformation patterns generalise across families
Investigate how parameter variation in function families underpins AI model training — discuss how adjusting model parameters changes predicted behaviour (conceptual, not technical)
Compare transformations across function families: which parameters shift, which stretch, which reflect — construct a generalisation that works across multiple function types
elaborations: investigating transformations of y=x to y=ax+b by systematic variation of a and b
investigating transformations of y=x² using digital tools, including completed square form; e.g. y=(1/3)(x−5)²+7
experimenting with reciprocal, square root, cube and exponential function families, identifying transformation patterns
investigating how parameter variation provides AI researchers insights into the predictive behaviour of AI models

AC9M9M01.minimum_width: Calculate the surface area and volume of one right prism and one cylinder using formulas; use appropriate units throughout.
AC9M9M01.typical_width: Calculate surface area and volume of a range of right prisms (triangular, rectangular, other polygonal cross-sections) and cylinders; analyse nets to understand how surface area formulas are derived; solve practical problems involving surface area and volume (e.g. material needed for a container, volume of a tank).
wider: Investigate objects and technologies of First Nations Australians (e.g. woven containers, bark canoes), analysing their surface area and volume, and exploring how these relate to capacity and function
Investigate the relationship between surface area and volume for prisms of fixed volume — conjecture about which prism shape minimises surface area and test using examples
Design a practical container for a given purpose (e.g. can-cooler, storage box) and determine the most material-efficient dimensions
elaborations: analysing nets of objects to generate shortcuts and establish formulas for surface area
determining the amount of material needed to make can-coolers; working out the most cost-efficient cutting approach
finding different prisms with the same volume but different surface areas; conjecturing about which prism has smallest or largest surface area
investigating objects and technologies of First Nations Australians, analysing surface area and volume, and exploring their relationship to capacity

AC9M9M02.minimum_width: Convert one very large and one very small measurement between decimal form and scientific notation; perform one calculation with values in scientific notation.
AC9M9M02.typical_width: Represent very large and very small measurements in scientific notation and convert back to decimal form; apply exponent laws to operate with numbers in scientific notation in applied contexts; use scientific notation in contexts from science and engineering (e.g. geological time scales, molecular masses); record measurements to the correct degree of accuracy.
wider: Investigate degrees of accuracy across different measurement instruments (e.g. measuring cylinder vs pipette) and discuss the relationship between instrument precision and scientific notation
Explore time scales in astronomy or geology — compare orders of magnitude and discuss how scientific notation makes these scales tractable
Investigate how computing systems represent and store very large or very small floating-point numbers, connecting to scientific notation
elaborations: representing very large and small real numbers in scientific notation; converting between forms; e.g. geological age of earth 4.6×10⁹ years, sugar molecule mass 5.68×10⁻²¹ grams
using place value knowledge and exponent laws to operate with numbers in scientific notation in applied contexts
examining the degree of accuracy of different measurement instruments (e.g. measuring cylinder vs pipette) and recording data using appropriate scientific notation

AC9M9M03.minimum_width: Apply Pythagoras' theorem and one trigonometric ratio (sin, cos or tan) to find an unknown side or angle in a right-angled triangle in a practical context.
AC9M9M03.typical_width: Apply Pythagoras' theorem, the three trigonometric ratios, similarity and scale to solve a range of spatial problems; use the scale factor relationship for areas of similar figures; apply the distance formula on the Cartesian plane; solve multi-step problems combining these tools.
wider: Apply Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to surveying or design problems — e.g. design and use a Biltmore stick to estimate tree height, connecting to rates and algebra
Investigate how autonomous vehicles solve spatial navigation problems using geometric properties (angles, distances, scale)
Explore applications of Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry in First Nations Australian navigation, astronomy or construction contexts
elaborations: investigating applications of Pythagoras' theorem in authentic problems, including surveying and design
applying the distance formula on the Cartesian plane
understanding the relationship between corresponding sides of similar right-angled triangles and the scale factor for areas
using photographic images to estimate actual measurements using scale
investigating the triangle inequality and generalising links between Pythagoras and inequalities for acute/obtuse triangles
designing and using a Biltmore stick using similar triangles, Pythagoras, rates and algebra
investigating how autonomous vehicles solve spatial problems using algorithms based on geometric properties

AC9M9M04.minimum_width: Calculate the absolute error and percentage error for one measurement in a practical context; explain what the error value means.
AC9M9M04.typical_width: Calculate and interpret absolute, relative and percentage errors across a range of measurement contexts (event attendance, budgets, laboratory instruments); use the absolute value formula for percentage error; give suitable lower and upper bounds for a measurement; recognise that all measurements are estimates.
wider: Investigate how AI systems (e.g. regression models, recommendation systems) use error metrics and discuss how the concepts of absolute and relative error apply in these contexts
Compare measurement errors across different instruments in a science lab context (e.g. measuring cylinders, rulers, digital scales) and discuss which instrument is appropriate for which task
Investigate percentage error in real-world budget or planning contexts — explore when overestimation vs underestimation of error has greater consequences
elaborations: investigating error as a percentage of the exact value
using absolute value in a percentage error formula; considering when to use absolute value depending on context
calculating percentage errors in expected budgets versus actual expenditure
estimating the accuracy of measurements in practical contexts and giving suitable lower and upper bounds
investigating how absolute, relative and percentage errors relate to AI systems such as regression models and recommendation systems

AC9M9M05.minimum_width: Formulate one practical problem involving direct proportion or rates as a mathematical model; solve it; interpret the solution in context; identify one assumption or limitation.
AC9M9M05.typical_width: Apply the full modelling cycle to at least two different practical contexts involving direct proportion, rates, ratio or scale; justify model choices; interpret solutions in terms of the situation; evaluate the model and report methods and findings.
wider: Explore fire management techniques used by First Nations Australians that involve proportion relationships — model the rate of fire spread in different fuel types relative to wind speed, temperature and humidity
Model compliance situations in building and construction (staircase rise-to-tread ratio, escalator gradient) and evaluate whether a design meets standards
Investigate image distortion in social media editing — model how non-uniform scaling breaks proportional relationships and calculate the resulting distortion
elaborations: modelling situations involving direct proportion: pro rata pay, exchange rates, multiple quotes, unit conversion, Hooke's law
modelling image editing on social media where proportion is not maintained, resulting in distorted images
modelling compliance with building and construction standards; e.g. staircase rise and tread, escalator components
modelling rates in practical contexts; e.g. density, birth rate, flow, heartbeats
exploring fire management techniques used by First Nations Australians using proportion relationships including rate of fire spread vs wind speed, temperature and humidity

AC9M9SP01.minimum_width: Identify the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse sides relative to a given angle in a right-angled triangle; verify using at least two similar triangles that the ratio of two specified sides is constant for a given angle; name that ratio as sine, cosine or tangent.
AC9M9SP01.typical_width: Establish, through investigation of nested similar triangles, that sine, cosine and tangent ratios are constant for a given angle regardless of triangle size; relate each ratio to the sides of the unit-hypotenuse triangle; connect the tangent of an angle to the gradient of a line on the Cartesian plane.
wider: Investigate how the tangent ratio connects to gradient — explore how the angle a line makes with the horizontal axis determines its gradient
Explore historical and cultural contexts for trigonometry (e.g. ancient surveying, astronomical measurement) and discuss how the constancy of ratios was understood before formal notation
Connect trig ratios to the unit circle informally — explore how sine and cosine values change as an angle increases from 0° to 90°
elaborations: understanding the terms base, altitude, hypotenuse, adjacent and opposite in a right-angled triangle
investigating patterns in nested similar triangles to identify constancy of ratios of corresponding sides for a given angle
establishing that sine is the altitude and cosine is the base of a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse of length one unit
relating tangent to altitude and base of nested similar triangles; connecting to gradient of a straight line

AC9M9SP02.minimum_width: Apply the enlargement transformation to one shape using a given scale factor; identify which properties remain invariant (angles, shape) and which change (lengths, area).
AC9M9SP02.typical_width: Apply enlargement transformations to 2D shapes and 3D objects using whole and rational scale factors; generalise the relationship between scale factor and changes to length (×k), area (×k²) and volume (×k³); use properties of similarity to solve problems.
wider: Investigate enlargement in design and mapping contexts — e.g. scale drawings, map scales, architectural plans — and discuss how scale factor relates to real-world measurements
Explore how image compression and digital zoom use enlargement transformations and discuss the trade-offs between scale and quality
Connect the area and volume scaling relationships (k² and k³) to biological scaling problems — e.g. why animals of different sizes have proportionally different limb thicknesses
elaborations: comparing the ratio of lengths of corresponding sides of similar triangles and angles
using the properties of similarity to solve problems involving enlargement
investigating and generalising patterns in length, angle, area and volume when side lengths are enlarged by whole and rational numbers; e.g. factor of 3 multiplies area by 9 and volume by 27

AC9M9SP03.minimum_width: Design an algorithm (pseudocode or flowchart) for one geometric construction or theorem application; test it with at least one case; identify one refinement needed.
AC9M9SP03.typical_width: Design, test and refine algorithms for at least two different geometric construction or theorem contexts (e.g. triangle inequality, angle bisection, Pythagorean triple generation); evaluate refinements by discussing how the algorithm improved; represent algorithms using pseudocode or flowcharts.
wider: Develop an algorithm for animating a geometric construction or visual proof; evaluate using multiple test cases and document refinements
Investigate how geometric algorithms underpin computer graphics or game development — discuss how specific geometric constructions (e.g. collision detection, rotation) are implemented algorithmically
Design an algorithm that verifies a geometric theorem (e.g. triangle inequality) for all integer side lengths up to a given bound and analyse its output
elaborations: creating an algorithm using pseudocode or flow charts to apply the triangle inequality, or to generate Pythagorean triples
creating and testing algorithms to construct or bisect angles
developing an algorithm for an animation of a geometric construction or visual proof; evaluating using test cases

AC9M9ST01.minimum_width: Analyse one statistical report to identify how data was obtained; assess whether the sampling method is likely to produce a representative sample; explain how this affects the reliability of any reported mean or median.
AC9M9ST01.typical_width: Analyse reports from a range of media sources; evaluate sampling methods, data collection procedures and the reasonableness of claims about population means and medians; link statistical claims back to data displays and assess whether the evidence supports the inference.
wider: Investigate statistical reports on Australia's trade with Asia-region countries — evaluate whether the data sources and methods support the claims made
Explore how NLP tools are used to analyse large volumes of survey reports; discuss the benefits and limitations of automated analysis for statistical interpretation
Analyse a range of data about different populations (e.g. age distributions in Australia, Cambodia and Tonga) and evaluate what can and cannot be inferred from the reported statistics
elaborations: investigating and evaluating statistical reports in the media by linking claims to displays, statistics and representative data
investigating the use of statistics in reports about Australia's trade with Asia region countries
exploring how NLP tools can be used to analyse large volumes of survey reports, discussing benefits and limitations
investigating a range of data and its sources; e.g. age of residents in Australia, Cambodia and Tonga; subjects studied by 14-year-olds across multiple countries
analysing reports of public opinion surveys on environmental issues; discussing data collection methods and the reasonableness of inferences

AC9M9ST02.minimum_width: Identify one sampling method used in a survey and explain one way it could introduce bias; identify one visualisation choice that could be used to make data appear to support a particular view.
AC9M9ST02.typical_width: Analyse how at least two different sampling methods (e.g. voluntary response, convenience, random) affect survey results; examine how visual choices (axis scale, graph type, omitted data) can be used to support a particular point of view; evaluate data visualisations (including infographics) for strengths, weaknesses and biases.
wider: Explore potential cultural bias in sampling techniques used in statistical reports about First Nations Australians — analyse specific reports and evaluate whether sampling methods are equitable and representative

Investigate how technological and social changes (e.g. reduced landline usage, call aversion) create new sources of sampling bias — discuss what kinds of populations are systematically under-represented
Analyse two infographics presenting the same data set and evaluate how different design choices lead to different interpretations
elaborations: investigating and analysing different visualisations of data (infographics in media), commenting on strengths, weaknesses and possible biases
discussing the impact of decreased landline usage or aversion to answering calls from unknown numbers on survey data
exploring potential cultural bias relating to First Nations Australians by critically analysing sampling techniques in statistical reports

AC9M9ST03.minimum_width: Represent two data sets using the same comparative display type (e.g. back-to-back stem-and-leaf, parallel box plots); describe and compare the distributions using at least two of: centre, spread, shape.
AC9M9ST03.typical_width: Represent multiple data sets using appropriate comparative representations; compare distributions with consideration of centre (mean, median), spread (range, IQR), shape (symmetric, skewed, bimodal) and the effect of outliers on each measure; construct and interpret grouped histograms.
wider: Explore comparative data from the National Indigenous Australians Agency 'Closing the Gap' reports; discuss the comparative distributions in context and what can and cannot be concluded from the data
Investigate how the same data set looks different when plotted using different representation types (stem-and-leaf vs histogram vs box plot) and discuss the trade-offs
Investigate a health dataset (e.g. disease incidence rates) using grouped histograms and evaluate what the distribution reveals about trends across the population
elaborations: describing the shape of data distributions using terms: positive skew, negative skew, symmetric, bi-modal
using stem-and-leaf plots to compare 2 like sets of data; e.g. heights of girls and boys
constructing grouped histograms showing trends in health issues and using them to justify, verify or invalidate claims
exploring comparative data from the National Indigenous Australians Agency 'Closing the Gap' reports; discussing comparative distributions in context

AC9M9ST04.minimum_width: Choose an appropriate display for one given data set (specifying data type as categorical or numerical, discrete or continuous); justify the choice; interpret one key feature of the display.
AC9M9ST04.typical_width: Choose appropriate display types for a range of data types (categorical nominal/ordinal, numerical discrete/continuous); justify selections with reference to data type, purpose and audience; interpret displays including stacked bar charts, area charts, line graphs, histograms, dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots; use digital tools to generate and compare displays.
wider: Evaluate non-standard visualisations such as infographics — assess purpose, intended audience and how well they communicate the statistical question
Use generative AI tools to produce multiple display options for a data set and critically evaluate which form best serves the intended purpose
Investigate how stacked bar charts and area charts represent part-whole relationships and compare their effectiveness against alternative display types for the same data
elaborations: comparing data displays using mean, median and range to describe and interpret numerical data sets using histograms, dot plots or stem-and-leaf plots
choosing representation type based on data type: categorical (nominal or ordinal) or numerical (discrete or continuous)
using non-standard representations such as infographics; evaluating how well they communicate for intended audiences
comparing and interpreting stacked bar charts, area charts and line graphs
using digital tools including generative AI to generate different data displays and discussing which form is most appropriate

AC9M9ST05.minimum_width: Pose one statistical question; collect or access data relevant to it; represent and analyse the data; report one finding and identify one limitation of the evidence.
AC9M9ST05.typical_width: Plan and conduct a statistical investigation with a clear question, appropriate data collection or secondary source selection, analysis using suitable representations and summary statistics, a report of findings, and an honest discussion of what the evidence does and does not support.
wider: Pose statistical questions relating to reconciliation and First Nations Australian communities; collect, represent and interpret data from different sources, considering relationships between variables

Conduct a multi-variable investigation (e.g. best location for a tropical fruit plantation) using secondary data from multiple sources; compare variables across countries or regions and evaluate the strength of evidence
Design and conduct a consumer research investigation (e.g. teenage spending habits) with attention to sample techniques, potential bias and the strength of conclusions that can be drawn
elaborations: planning and conducting an investigation using secondary data from online databases such as the ABS
planning and conducting an investigation relating to consumer spending habits; modelling market research on teenage spending with consideration of sample techniques and potential bias
investigating the best location for a tropical fruit plantation by comparing variables such as annual rainfall in Australia, Indonesia, New Guinea and Malaysia, land prices and farming costs
posing statistical questions, collecting, representing and interpreting data in relation to reconciliation, considering relationships between variables

AC9M9P01.minimum_width: List all outcomes for one two-step compound event (with or without replacement) using a systematic method (tree diagram, table or list); assign probabilities to the outcomes.
AC9M9P01.typical_width: List all outcomes for compound events both with and without replacement using tree diagrams, tables and arrays; assign probabilities to all outcomes; compare how replacing or not replacing changes the probability space; extend to three-stage events using tree diagrams.
wider: Investigate two-step games and competitions (e.g. selecting team leaders from a bag) — use systematic listing to assign exact probabilities and compare to intuitive estimates
Explore compound events involving real population data (e.g. selecting 2 students from a school year group) and discuss how probabilities change with population size
Connect compound event probability to combinatorial reasoning — introduce the idea of counting outcomes systematically as a foundation for future work with permutations and combinations
elaborations: discussing two-step chance experiments such as Heads and Tails, describing outcomes and probabilities
using systematic methods (lists or arrays) to record outcomes and assign probabilities
using a tree diagram for a three-stage event; e.g. selecting 3 cards with and without replacement
assigning probabilities to compound events involving random selection from a population; e.g. selecting 2 Year 9 students at random from a school

AC9M9P02.minimum_width: Calculate relative frequencies from a given data set to estimate the probability of one event involving 'and' or 'or'; represent the event using a Venn diagram or two-way table.
AC9M9P02.typical_width: Use relative frequencies from given or collected data to estimate probabilities of events involving 'and', inclusive 'or' and exclusive 'or'; represent compound events using Venn diagrams and two-way tables; connect long-run relative frequency to theoretical probability.
wider: Design, test and refine an algorithm to calculate relative frequencies from a generated data set — use the algorithm to estimate probabilities for compound events and evaluate its reliability
Investigate how large data sets (e.g. health survey data, census data) are used to estimate population-level probabilities — discuss the role of sample size in reliability
Connect Venn diagram regions to set notation ('and' = intersection, 'or' = union) as a foundation for formal probability
elaborations: understanding that relative frequencies from large data sets or long-run experiments provide reliable probability estimates
using Venn diagrams or two-way tables to estimate frequencies of events involving 'and' and 'or'
designing, testing and refining an algorithm to determine relative frequencies from a generated data set to estimate different probabilities

AC9M9P03.minimum_width: Design and conduct one chance experiment or simulation using a digital tool; compare the experimental probability of one simple event to a related compound event; describe the result.
AC9M9P03.typical_width: Design and conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations using digital tools; compare probabilities of simple events to related compound events; compare experiments that differ only by with/without replacement; use systematic methods to list favourable outcomes; describe and explain results.
wider: Use repeated trials of First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Gorri) to calculate probabilities of winning and not winning — compare experimental results to theoretical predictions
Design a simulation to investigate a counterintuitive probability result (e.g. birthday problem, Monty Hall problem at an accessible level) and use the simulation to build intuition
Investigate how simulation is used in real-world contexts (e.g. risk modelling, weather forecasting) to estimate probabilities that are too complex to calculate theoretically
elaborations: using digital tools to conduct probability simulations demonstrating the relationship between compound event and individual probabilities
comparing experiments that differ only by with vs without replacement
conducting two-step chance experiments using systematic methods to list outcomes
using repeated trials of First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Gorri) to calculate probabilities of winning and not winning
